1.pericope_label: Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not; The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots. The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses:

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep the woe and use it to mark the structure of what follows: the city has brought this fate on itself, can no more avert it than a great Egyptian city could, and comes at last to a terrible end; they treat the two nouns as accusatives without a conjunction, the first meaning deceit, and have the prophet see the hostile army burst upon the city and hear the charioteers' whips. Ellicott renders the opening as an address rather than a woe, and turns the battle picture into exclamations, hark to the whip and to the rattling wheel, the horse galloping and the chariot bounding: the entry of the victorious besiegers.

Gill notes that the opening term is vocative, so that the Greek renders it as an address, and makes the whip that of a driver urging his horses to reach the city, heard by the inhabitants and so the more terrible. Calvin calls the exclamation emphatic and reads it as though the prophet were constraining the city to undergo its punishment; he observes that the two nouns, one signifying leanness and the other to lay by, seem to differ widely and yet both denote spoil, and on the clause about the prey he prefers a continued licence in plundering to the reading that it shall not be withdrawn from the conquerors' hands.

Clarke turns the battle picture into a rhapsody, hearing the whip crack and the wheels rumble, seeing the chariots bound after the galloping steeds, the spears like gashes of lightning, and the slain in heaps with horses stumbling over them, then breaking off to call war infernal and add that it is sometimes the scourge of the Lord. Wesley identifies the horsemen as the Chaldeans and their confederates.

Henry draws the whole into an indictment of five counts, and neither numbers nor grandeur will secure the place from prosecution: blood shed by unrighteous war or under colour of justice; lies, so that no man knows whom to trust; rapine, nobody caring what mischief he does or to whom; idolatries, by which she defiled herself and seduced her neighbours; and witchcrafts, by which, aiming at universal monarchy, she used arts as well as arms and courted other nations into her rites. For this God has a quarrel with her, since he who made of one blood all nations never designed one to be a nation of tyrants and another of slaves.

debates.question: Do the second and third verses describe the invading army or the state of the city?

positions.position: The entry of the victorious besiegers.
The state of the city in the prophet's own day; the sacking has already been set out, and what follows gives the reason for it.
The enemy's approach, heard by the inhabitants.

debates.question: How is the opening word to be taken?

positions.position: As a vocative address, O bloody city, following the Greek.
As an emphatic exclamation, constraining the city to undergo its punishment.
As a woe, opening the last section of the threatening prophecy.

outliers.claim: Offers his own version of the three verses against the common reading, deriving one verb from a root meaning to feel after a thing in order to explore it, reading one phrase as a multitude dancing or piping against the dead mass of the slain, and proposing that a letter in another word is a copyist's mistake.

themes: Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not;
The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots.

The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses:

4.pericope_label: Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts. Behold, I am against thee, saith the Lord of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame. And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock. And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?

schools.summary: Ellicott adds a reason for the flight of those who look on, that men run from the stricken city lest they share her punishment, and holds that one whose cruelties were as wide as her empire is no object of compassion, closing with two lines of verse on the fallen tyrant left to groan unpitied and alone. Keil and Delitzsch keep the gazing-stock of the received version without comment.

Gill points, with Clarke, to the custom behind the filth cast at her, the dirt thrown at women set in the pillory or carted; and he pursues the epithet of the harlot into the name of the city, which two scholars derive from a word for a pleasant habitation, recalling too that the queen from whose husband it is thought to be named was first a harlot of surpassing beauty. Calvin makes the change of speaker at the fifth verse the point, God testifying that the Assyrians have no strife with any mortal but with their own judgment, since the Chaldeans do not break in of themselves but are guided by a hidden providence; on the stripping he observes that a harlot's dress conceals what she is, and that God will strip the city of the magnificence that has blinded her.

Clarke notes that the city was figured a moment ago as a lion tearing all in pieces and is now a beautiful prostitute enticing all men into idolatry, says it was an ancient though not a laudable practice to strip such women and expose them to public execration, and answers the closing question from her deserts, that she was the occasion of ruin to multitudes. Wesley allows both senses of the whoredoms, the idolatries and the literal vice, glosses the witchcrafts as bewitching policies or necromancy, reads the stripping as the treatment inhuman soldiers give captive women, and asks whose bowels will be moved for her that had none for anyone.

debates.question: How should the last word of the sixth verse be rendered?

positions.position: As a spectacle or example; the rendering dung, after the Rabbins, is wrong, since the word comes from the verb to see.
As a gazing-stock, with the received version.

debates.question: Why will no one bewail her?

positions.position: Because she deserves none: she ruined multitudes and had no bowels for anyone.
Because men flee lest they share her punishment, and her cruelties were as wide as her empire.
Not from her deserts at all: the calamity is so great that no lamentation could equal it, though all the world wept.

outliers.claim: Traces the epithet of the well-favoured harlot into the etymology of the city's name, which two scholars derive from a word for a beautiful or pleasant habitation, and recalls that the queen from whose husband the city is generally thought to be named was herself first a harlot of surpassing beauty.

themes: Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts.
Behold, I am against thee, saith the Lord of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame.
And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock.
And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?

8.pericope_label: Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea? Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers. Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains.

schools.summary: Ellicott names the great southern capital of Egypt and explains the Hebrew form as the house of the god whose name it carries; he alone marshals the Assyrian records, listing three campaigns with their dates and the booty carried to Nineveh, and draws from it that the fall being already past when the prophet wrote, the allusion helps fix the date of the book. He then builds the comparison clause by clause: if the one city was protected by its rivers, had not the other a rampart in the great river and its canals. Keil and Delitzsch render the two verses through and state the moral in a line, that the fate of the one city is a prophecy of the other's.

Gill reports the Targum and three Jewish commentators taking the city for Alexandria but leans himself to the great city of the south, famous in the old poet for its hundred gates, noting that some think that number was not of gates but of temples; on the date he reports one Jewish authority that the Chaldean king took it on his way to Nineveh, remarks that when and by whom is nowhere said, and cites two chronologers who assign the sack to the Assyrian king who harassed Egypt three years together. Calvin, who takes the city for Alexandria throughout, dwells on the treatment of the captives.

Clarke puts the city in the Delta on one branch of the river, so that it had the fork of two branches to defend it by land and the sea for a barrier and was wholly surrounded by water; he supposes it destroyed lately, probably by the Chaldeans, locates the further two allied peoples in Africa and Libya, and reports the custom of casting lots among the commanders, with the great men kept in chains to grace the triumph. Wesley proceeds as though the city were Alexandria and makes one ally the Moors west of it, glossing the boast of infinite strength as meaning there was no end to their confidence and provision.

Henry takes the prophet to be quoting precedents to break a false confidence, the city having said in effect that she should have peace, and draws the moral that it keeps us in a holy fear to consider we are no better than those who fell before us; he adds the trade as well as the auxiliary troops to the fallen city's strength, and calls the place fortified by nature and art at once, the river both watering the fields and guarding the wall.

debates.question: Which Egyptian city is the one held up as a precedent?

positions.position: Alexandria, with the Targum and the Jewish commentators.
The great city of the south, famous for its hundred gates.
A city of the Delta, on one branch of the river and surrounded by water.

debates.question: When did that city fall, and to whom?

positions.position: Lately, and probably to the Chaldeans.
In one of three datable Assyrian campaigns, the last of which certainly sacked it.
When and by whom is nowhere said, though two chronologers assign it to the Assyrian king who harassed Egypt three years together.

outliers.claim: Explains the casting of lots from ancient practice, that when two captors disputed a prisoner the lot decided whose he should be, and finds it remarkable that lots were cast here on the princes, a thing usually reserved for the lowest slaves.

themes: Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?
Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers.

Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains.

11.pericope_label: Thou also shalt be drunken: thou shalt be hid, thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy. All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater. Behold, thy people in the midst of thee are women: the gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies: the fire shall devour thy bars. Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains how the irony of the fourteenth verse works: the city is scoffingly told to protract her resistance, to hold out in the citadel now the outer walls are down, to lay in water and build new buttresses, and in the middle of those preparations fire and sword will surprise her; he observes that the account is minute on purpose and compares another prophet who, describing the making of an idol, goes back to the smith at his tongs and the carpenter at his rule. On the people called women he denies that the phrase refers to their luxurious habits and refers it to their panic at the catastrophe. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses through and say the prophet is taking away the last prop of the city's hope, its fortifications and its numbers.

Gill notes with Wesley that the first ripe fruit is loosened by the least shake, so the fortresses they trusted in would fall as easily; he reads the people called women of a settled character, weak and timorous and fleeing at the first approach of the enemy, with some regard to their king's effeminacy; and he says briefly of the ironical advice that they might do what they would and it would all be in vain. Calvin makes the emphatic particle of the eleventh verse carry the argument, since God continues ever like himself and is judge of the world to the end; he inclines to read the hiding as a vanishing away rather than a hiding for shame, generalises the figs into the doctrine that whatever strength men gather will vanish, and rejects the construction that would make one verb mean to hold or lay hold.

Clarke turns the metaphor of the figs into history: at the first shock all the strongholds were abandoned and the king in despair burnt himself and his household in his palace. He is the only one who has handled the materials, explaining that the river ran near so that they are told to lay in fresh water against a long siege, describing the ancient brickmaking of that country, and adding that he has some of those very bricks before him as he writes, hard yet wholly soluble in water, with others that appear kiln-burnt. Wesley calls the people cowards and takes the gates for the frontier fortresses, opened by fear or treachery.

debates.question: What does it mean that the city shall be hid?

positions.position: That she will vanish away as though she had never been, since to be hidden often means in Hebrew to be reduced to nothing.
That she will hide herself for shame and sue to others for help.

debates.question: Why are the people called women?

positions.position: For a settled character, weak and timorous, with some regard to the king's effeminacy.
Not for their luxurious habits at all, but for their panic-stricken condition at the catastrophe.

outliers.claim: Describes the ancient brickmaking of that country from the artefacts themselves, and adds that he has some of those very bricks lying before him as he writes, hard yet wholly soluble in water, with others made without straw that appear to have been burnt in a kiln.

themes: Thou also shalt be drunken: thou shalt be hid, thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy.
All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater.
Behold, thy people in the midst of thee are women: the gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies: the fire shall devour thy bars.
Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln.

15.pericope_label: There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts. Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and flieth away. Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are. Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust: thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the three insect words stand for varieties of one species and explains the behaviour against Clarke's account, a burst of sunshine sending a swarm into flight while cold makes them settle and takes from them the power of flying; he takes the crowned for the subordinate kings who represented the empire in its provinces, the word rendered captains for an Assyrian term of high military rank, the shepherds for chief officers, and would read the clause about the nobles not that they shall dwell but that they lie still. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses and sum up the kingdom's end in a line.

Gill leaves the fire open, taking it for the fire of divine wrath, or what the enemy would put in, or, with a Jewish commentator and the Targum, the enemy himself; he canvasses who the crowned are and then leaves the exposition altogether to establish that locusts really do wear crowns; and he alone tries to settle who the last Assyrian king was, taking two of the three names given by the historians for the same man. Calvin makes the adverb of place the sting of the fifteenth verse, since the Lord would turn the very defences they trusted in to their destruction, and takes the shepherds for the counsellors in whose wisdom the king trusted.

Clarke refers the reader to his notes on an earlier prophet for the locusts in their various states, calls the successive swarms the most expressive simile for the successive armies, says they shelter about the hedges in cold weather and forage in the heat, and makes the shepherds the rulers and tributary princes who deserted the city, supporting it from the historians. Wesley fixes the fire in the fortresses and turns the challenge back, that they may be as many as they can and it will be to no purpose, and agrees that the crowned are confederate kings whose number was all for show.

debates.question: How do locusts behave in heat and cold?

positions.position: They shelter about the hedges in cold weather and come out to forage when the sun is hot.
A burst of sunshine sends a swarm into flight, while cold makes them settle and soon takes from them the power of flying.

debates.question: Who are the shepherds that slumber?

positions.position: The counsellors in whose wisdom the king trusted, ridiculed for having no vigilance even for themselves.
The rulers and tributary princes who deserted the city in her distress.
Chief officers, whose sheep are scattered on the mountains with none to gather them.

outliers.claim: Leaves the exposition entirely at the seventeenth verse to establish that locusts really do wear crowns, citing a swarm out of the Turkish provinces into Austria and Silesia, an ancient writer on locusts in Arabia marked with gold-coloured figures, and the Targum's shining locust that shines like gold.

themes: There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts.
Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and flieth away.

Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are.
Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust: thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them.

19.pericope_label: There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the joy at the news universal and asks the question that justifies it, where her oppressive rule had not been felt; he observes that the verse is addressed to the king himself, in the second person masculine, as representative of the empire and perhaps with his own terrible end in view; and he alone illustrates the cruelty from the monuments rather than the text, quoting a modern writer on the sculptures with their rows of the impaled, prisoners with rings through their lips, and men blinded or flayed alive. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse through without comment.

Gill offers two senses of the wound, that there is no healing of the bruise or no contraction of it, as when a wound is nearly closed and the skin round about is wrinkled; he holds the blow given by the taking of the city irreparable, since the place was no more and the empire never rose again, and notes what the Targum makes of the verse. Calvin explains why the ruin is incurable before describing it, since the wicked harbour false expectations of gathering new strength; he dismisses the rendering of a wrinkle as improper, notes that the term is used elsewhere of restraining wickedness and of checking leprosy, and would read not that the wound is grievous but that the stroke is.

Clarke closes the chapter with a long quotation on the improbability of what happened, asking what likelihood there was that a city sixty miles in compass, with walls a hundred feet high and thick enough for three chariots abreast and fifteen hundred towers of two hundred feet, should be totally destroyed; yet the place is hardly known where it stood, the sacred writers mention it no more after the enlarging of Babylon, and writers are not agreed even about its situation. Wesley takes the clapping of hands for insult and rejoicing and the wickedness for the tyranny, pride and cruelty by which she trod her neighbours down.

debates.question: What does the word for the wound mean?

positions.position: Either no healing of the bruise or no contraction of it, as the skin wrinkles round a closing wound.
No stopping of the breach short of its becoming complete; the rendering of a wrinkle is improper.

debates.question: What is meant by the clapping of hands?

positions.position: Exultation and insult over the downfall.
Universal joy, since her oppressive rule had been felt everywhere.
Possibly not clapping at all: striking the hand is in Hebrew a token of consent, so all would express approbation of the judgment.

outliers.claim: Quotes at length a bishop's argument on the improbability of the city's total ruin, from its sixty-mile compass and hundred-foot walls to the fact that so little remains that writers are not agreed even about its situation, some placing it on one river and some on another.

themes: There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?
